newsitem.title: TAIWAN: CPC aims to reopen Taiwan crude port in one week.
newsitem.headline: CPC aims to reopen Taiwan crude port in one week.

text.p: State-owned Chinese Petroleum said on Thursday it was conducting pressure tests at its northern Taiwan oil port, which it shut down at the weekend, and aimed to reopen one of two offloading units within a week.
The oil tanker Vanadis, which has been waiting since Sunday to offload 300,000 tonnes of African crude, was assisting with the repair work, a Chinese Petroleum executive said.

"The repair team had the Vanadis pump water into one of the closed oil offloading units so that divers could check for leaks," the executive said from the company's adjacent Taoyuan refinery, which has been crippled by the port's closure.
He said the company expected to have one of the two units operating within a week but declined to give details.
Officials had said on Wednesday that strong currents had halted efforts to repair unspecified pipeline problems that shut down both of the port's offloading units at the weekend.
The company executive, reached by telephone, said divers had not been able to work for more than two hours but that they were making progress in repairing the problem.
The shutdown of the two offshore units cut off the flow of crude to the Taoyuan refinery, which in turn was forced to shut down one of its two distillation units to slow production.
The Taoyuan refinery produces 60,000 tonnes of jet fuel a month at full capacity while Chinese Petroleum's Kaohsiung plant can produce 60,000 to 80,000 tonnes, industry sources said.
Taiwan's main international airport at Taoyuan alone consumes 150,000 tonnes of aircraft fuel a month. Taiwan also has major airports in downtown Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung.
The Taoyuan refinery had been running at just 33 percent of capacity since the crude port was shut down.
Chinese Petroleum's purchase on Wednesday of a 32,000-tonne jet oil shipment was necessitated in part by the refinery's production slowdown, company officials said.
In Singapore, Chinese Petroleum sources said the company bought a second cargo of jet fuel on Thursday to compensate for shortages arising from the Taoyuan refinery's slowdown.
The seller confirmed that Chinese Petroleum awarded the 32,000-tonne cargo, for October 1-31 delivery, at $247.82 per tonne to a U.S. major.
CPC had earlier cancelled a tender to buy jet fuel for October delivery due to high offers ranging between just under $250 to over $260 per tonne, c-and-f basis, traders said.
